channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Passive tobacco smoke exposure linked to nonallergic atopic dermatitis severity in young children
item.description: Passive tobacco smoke exposure, particularly paternal smoking and postnatal household exposure, is associated with increased disease severity among children aged 0 to 2 years with nonallergic atopic dermatitis, according to a study published in Advances in Dermatology and Allergology.

item.title: Many women have never discussed heart health with a clinician, and most report multiple symptoms
item.description: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in women, and the risk rises during the menopause years. But an international study has revealed that only half of women know this. Many have never talked about their heart with a doctor or a nurse, and the majority are living with multiple symptoms.

item.title: The parts of fruits and vegetables most throw away could save your health—and the planet
item.description: Most of us routinely discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds of fruits and vegetables at mealtime. But new research from King's College London suggests these scraps could be a valuable—and overlooked—source of dietary fiber, offering potential benefits for both public health and the environment.

item.title: Long-term follow-up tracks benefits and risks of stem cell transplants for severe systemic sclerosis
item.description: An international study reports 60% progression-free survival at 10 years after autologous bone marrow transplantation, adding evidence of sustained positive clinical outcomes and long-term safety in patients treated for early severe systemic sclerosis.

item.title: Could a few bad dietary choices worsen your next immune response?
item.description: Scientists have long known that diet shapes the immune system. Now, a UC San Francisco team has found that even a brief dietary change can substantially change how the body responds to skin irritation, at least in mice.

item.title: Noninvasive tests detect advanced liver scarring and could reduce reliance on biopsies
item.description: Two major international studies have delivered the strongest evidence to date on which noninvasive tests can accurately diagnose and measure the severity of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and its more severe form, MASH, reducing reliance on liver biopsy.

item.title: How common dietary fats can aggravate chronic itch
item.description: A team of researchers has found that a breakdown product from a commonly consumed fat can bind to a receptor associated with psoriatic itch and inflammation. By blocking the receptor, the researchers saw a reduction in psoriatic itch in a mouse model. Published in the journal Communications Biology, the work demonstrates the potential impact of diet on chronic itch triggers and could lead to future therapies for both psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.

item.title: How psychedelics could deliver antidepressant benefits without hallucinogenic effects
item.description: Could psychedelics become a new generation of treatments for depression and other psychiatric disorders? This question is no longer confined to basic research. Several therapies based on classical psychedelics have advanced into late-stage clinical development and have reported encouraging results. DT120, an LSD-based candidate, and COMP360, a synthetic psilocybin formulation, have both received breakthrough therapy designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

item.title: Known for preventing cancer, p53 could also help immune cells fight it
item.description: Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a new strategy to make cancer-fighting immune cells stronger and potentially longer-lasting, a discovery that could help improve the effectiveness of immunotherapies that use a patient's own immune cells to attack cancer.

item.title: How insurance coverage shapes access to kidney transplantation
item.description: For people with kidney failure, access to transplantation can mean better survival and quality of life.

item.title: Xenon-based method measures key MRI contrast metal more sensitively than earlier techniques
item.description: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, provides detailed images of the inside of the body. It is an indispensable procedure for the diagnosis and treatment planning of many types of cancer, and it does not expose the body to radiation because it uses magnetic fields and low-energy radio waves. Pathological changes, such as tumors, can be clearly distinguished from healthy tissue in MRI images.

item.title: Spinal cord injury can reshape gut microbes that influence whole-body health
item.description: Scientists exploring the links between a spinal cord injury, inflammation and immune function have turned their attention to a genome-level analysis of the gut microbial community, with early study results offering hints at potential new approaches to aid healing.

item.title: ASN: Low protein intake linked to kidney failure risk in Asian patients with CKD
item.description: Among patients with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD), low protein intake is associated with an increased risk for kidney failure requiring replacement therapy (KFRT) and all-cause mortality, according to a study published online Oct. 22 in JAMA Network Open to coincide with Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

item.title: When things go bump in the night: How our brains trick us into hearing things that aren't there
item.description: It's 3 a.m. You've woken from a dead sleep because you've heard a thud in the darkness or a floorboard creaking downstairs. Or perhaps you've woken because you have the unmistakable sensation you're not alone.

item.title: Tumor mutations and immune activity may reveal who benefits from investigational lymphoma drug
item.description: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba conducted a physician-initiated phase 2 clinical trial of dasatinib in patients with relapsed or refractory T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (TFHL), an aggressive and difficult-to-treat blood cancer. The study identified genetic alterations and features of the immune microenvironment associated with treatment response. These findings may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit from dasatinib and inform the development of personalized treatment strategies and novel immunotherapeutic approaches. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

item.title: Immune system protein is a cancer killer on its own, new study shows
item.description: For decades, scientists have known that a protein made by T cells and natural killer (NK) cells in the immune system, called perforin, can kill tumor cells by punching a hole in the cell wall and injecting proteases called granzymes, which kill the cell. Now, new work led by researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center found that tumor cells could be killed even when major granzymes were missing.

item.title: Common gut virus infects bacteria—not human cells
item.description: Thriving alongside trillions of bacteria in the human digestive tract is a vast population of viruses. Ever since one such denizen of the gut microbiome, known as picobirnavirus, was first spotted decades ago, researchers thought it directly infected human tissue and played a role in gastrointestinal illness. But researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and collaborators have just rewritten that story: This widespread virus infects gut bacteria, not human cells.

item.title: Residential fine particulate matter linked to minimal residual disease in pediatric leukemia
item.description: For pediatric patients with high-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), residential fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) concentrations during induction therapy are associated with positive end-of-induction (EOI) minimal residual disease (MRD), according to a study published in JNCI Cancer Spectrum.

item.title: Ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime help resistant bacteria thrive in hospital sewage
item.description: Antibiotics excreted by patients promote antibiotic-resistant bacteria in hospital sewers, according to a new study by researchers at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden. Ultimately, this may contribute to the development and spread of hard-to-treat infections. Pinpointing the responsible antibiotics paves the way for targeted measures.

item.title: Heat waves and pollution increase stroke risk in older adults, study finds
item.description: A study conducted in Brazil by researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) found that each additional day spent under a heat wave in São Paulo is associated with an increased risk of acute stroke in people ages 65 and older. For the research, a heat wave was defined as at least two consecutive days with maximum temperatures of 33.1 °C (92 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher.

item.title: Why people with diabetes are more vulnerable to air pollution's cellular toll
item.description: Air pollution affects health beyond the lungs. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5), tiny airborne particles that can enter the respiratory system, can trigger inflammation that affects other parts of the body. People with type 2 diabetes may be particularly vulnerable, as the disease can already impair stem cell function in the bone marrow, which produces blood cells and supports bone health.

item.title: COMPASS pathway enables regulatory T cells to prevent devastating autoimmune responses to gut bacteria
item.description: Trillions of bacteria live in the human gut without triggering an immune response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have now discovered a gene-regulatory pathway that helps maintain this delicate balance. In a study published in Science Advances, they show that regulatory T cells, a type of immune cell, co-opt a well-known general gene expression pathway called COMPASS to suppress inappropriate immune responses and prevent lethal inflammation and autoimmunity.

item.title: Blood test offers new way to track lung cancer
item.description: Northwestern Medicine scientists and collaborators have demonstrated a novel liquid biopsy technique that can measure cancer burden and reveal molecular characteristics of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), according to a new study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

item.title: Fight, flight, focus: A pathway from exercise to cognition
item.description: It's a tried-and-true method for improving your focus: taking a break for a brisk walk.

item.title: Healthy diet may lower heart disease risk after cancer
item.description: Eating a healthy diet is associated with a reduced risk of heart disease and death among cancer survivors, according to a study published today in JACC: Advances.

item.title: Specialized immune cells may help skin nimbly respond to changing environmental conditions
item.description: As the steadfast protector of the body's interior, the skin must be able to swiftly respond to stressors from the outside world and then return to a steady state to maintain everyday operations. Coordinating that agile response are epidermal stem cells (EpSCs), which initiate development of specialized skin cells sent to the surface while also maintaining a ready pool of new stem cells to draw from.

item.title: Premature birth alters the brain's developmental clock
item.description: A new study reveals that when a baby is born prematurely, their cerebellum, the part of the brain with a critical role in motor function, language and cognition, grows and develops in a different way than it would if the baby remained in utero to full term.

item.title: Antibody candidate could help preserve appetite and muscle strength in patients with cancer
item.description: In cancer cachexia, patients continue to lose weight, muscle and fat even when they eat. A KAIST research team has developed a therapeutic candidate that blocks a signal responsible for appetite suppression, weight loss and excessive energy expenditure.

item.title: Lower serum total calcium linked to postdischarge outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: For hospitalized patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), low serum total calcium is associated with a reduced risk for heart failure readmission, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular events after discharge, according to a study published online Sept. 28 in Biomedicines.

item.title: 5 calisthenics moves for a full-body workout you can do anywhere
item.description: Whether you realize it or not, you're probably already familiar with calisthenics. Put simply, calisthenics is just bodyweight exercises. Calisthenics is great for beginners because it builds full-body strength and requires no equipment. You can also easily modify exercises for different levels of difficulty.
